title: Design language learning with artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots based on activity theory from a systematic review
extended_summary:
This paper reviews research on how AI chatbots are used in language learning and, more specifically, how different sociocultural and instructional factors shape student outcomes when chatbots are used in educational settings. The authors argue that prior reviews have focused too much on whether chatbots work and not enough on the mechanisms and contextual factors that explain why outcomes vary.

Using Activity Theory as the organizing framework, the review synthesizes 37 empirical studies published from January 2014 to January 2025. The studies included K–12 and higher education contexts, with most conducted in higher education and in traditional classroom settings. The review examines the roles of rules/course design, tools/chatbots, community, and division of labor among students, teachers, peer students, researchers, and the AI systems themselves.

The review concludes that chatbot-supported language learning produces four main outcome types: cognitive, emotional, behavioral, and agentic. Cognitive outcomes were most common, followed by emotional and behavioral outcomes, while agentic outcomes were least frequent and especially underexplored. The authors find that outcomes are shaped by instructional design, teacher support, chatbot capabilities, and the degree of collaboration and feedback in the activity system. They recommend stronger teacher-AI collaboration models, more professional language-education chatbots, and more research in K–12 settings, collaborative learning, and agentic outcomes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI chatbots/LLM-based assistants used for conversational language support, feedback, and task completion.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a systematic review of 37 studies on AI chatbots in language learning, including generic GenAI tools and named products; it also discusses teacher-AI collaboration, prompt-like instructional design, and risks.

findings.finding_summary: Across 37 reviewed studies, chatbot-supported language learning was associated mainly with cognitive outcomes (43% of studies) and emotional outcomes (38%), with some behavioral (15%) and agentic outcomes (4%). The review synthesizes that well-designed course rules, teacher support, and chatbot-mediated interaction can help students attain language-learning outcomes, though the paper does not report pooled effect sizes.
findings.measure: Reported frequency and thematic synthesis of learning outcomes across reviewed studies

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that most studies found improved linguistic performance and language knowledge, especially in writing, speaking, listening, reading, pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammatical accuracy. It also notes that some studies found no significant improvement in listening performance, and one study found higher GPA students did not write significantly better with a chatbot than with traditional instruction.
findings.measure: Language performance/achievement in writing, speaking, listening, reading, pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that chatbot-supported learning often increased motivation, confidence, willingness to communicate, enjoyment, and positive attitudes, while lowering anxiety in many studies. It also highlights a four-staged ChatGPT-based rapport-building protocol that was reported to improve teacher-student rapport and L2 grit, but no effect size was given in the review text.
findings.measure: Motivation, attitude, confidence, willingness to communicate, enjoyment/interest, anxiety, and grit

findings.finding_summary: The review identifies behavioral gains such as increased language practice frequency, greater class engagement, and more frequent or varied interactions with chatbots. It also notes a small set of agentic outcomes, including using English for realistic purposes and proactively seeking information or help from the chatbot when encountering unfamiliar content.
findings.measure: Language practice frequency, class engagement, interaction frequency/types, and agentic behaviors

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing prior studies rather than a single empirical intervention or meta-analysis with pooled effects. The evidence is useful for mapping patterns, but it does not provide primary causal estimates for one tool.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broadly positive associations between chatbot use and several language-learning outcomes, but it reports no effect sizes or pooled estimates. The impact is therefore directionally promising but quantitatively unclear.
